label: Unit 1
themeSub: Steps, in order, and the bug you go back and fix
intro: Nothing here is about a screen. Programming at four is three ideas: instructions happen in the order you gave them, the machine does what you said instead of what you meant, and a thing that went wrong is a thing you go back and change. Code the Bee is the whole unit in one game — he builds the program before anything runs, and a bad run leaves it on screen so the next tap is a fix rather than a guess.

gelds.text: Puts steps in order and can say which one comes first
Gives an instruction exact enough to follow — three steps, not "over there"
Plans the whole thing before starting it
Finds his own mistake and changes that one step
Spots a repeat, and can say what comes next because of it

tryNote: The robot game at the top is the one to do first, and it works anywhere — hallway, driveway, grocery aisle. You are the robot. Be a very literal robot.

daily.title: You be the robot
daily.do: He gives you instructions to get across the room. You do EXACTLY what he says, in order, and nothing else. "Go" gets you walking into the wall. He'll laugh, then he'll get specific.
daily.stretch: He has to say all the steps BEFORE you start moving, and then you run them all without stopping. That's the difference between telling somebody what to do and writing a program.
daily.skill: Plan the whole thing, then run it

daily.title: Find the broken step
daily.do: Tell him a four-step routine he knows, with one step in the wrong place: put your shoes on, walk outside, put your socks on, get in the car. "Which one is wrong?"
daily.stretch: He fixes it by MOVING one step rather than starting the list over. Finding which step is wrong is the skill; redoing the whole thing is avoiding it.

daily.title: Say it once, do it four times
daily.do: Instead of "scrub, scrub, scrub, scrub," say "scrub four times." Then let him give you one: one instruction, a number of times. That's a loop, and he'll use the word if you do.
daily.stretch: Ask him for something that repeats until something else happens: pour until the cup is full. Until is a different idea from four times, and it's the harder one.
daily.skill: Repeat a number of times, or until

goalsTitle: What he should have by the end of this unit

his: Builds a three or four step program before pressing Run, instead of tapping and hoping
Says up, down, left and right and means them
Fixes a program that bumped instead of clearing the whole thing
Says "there's a bug" about a mistake — his or anybody's — without it meaning he failed
Puts a four-step routine in order with no prompting

weekend: Let him direct you making his sandwich, step by step, and follow it literally. Bread on the plate is not the same instruction as bread out of the bag. That's the funniest twenty minutes in the unit and it teaches the whole thing.

songs.title: Step by Step
songs.style: A playful preschool sing-along with plucky pizzicato strings, toy piano and light hand claps. Slow, steady tempo a four-year-old can sing with, one warm friendly voice, a simple repeated melody, every word clear. Singing starts within the first two seconds, and it ends cleanly with no long outro.
lyrics: Step by step, one at a time —
Tell it up, tell it down,
The bee does what I say,
not what I meant to say.
If it bumps into a wall,
I don't quit, I go back,
I press run and watch it go —
my bee found the flower. Buzz, buzz!

lines.start: Tell the bee how to get to the flower.
lines.wall: The bee bumped into something. Fix your program and try again.
lines.stop: The bee stopped in the wrong place. Fix your program and try again.

advanced.label: Step
advanced.note: A step is one thing you tell the computer to do.

advanced.label: Program
advanced.note: A program is all your steps, in the order you want them.

advanced.label: Loop
advanced.note: A loop is doing the same step again and again.

advanced.label: Bug
advanced.note: A bug is a step that came out wrong. Everybody makes them.

advanced.label: Fix
advanced.note: Fixing means finding the one step that was wrong and changing it.

advanced.label: Run
advanced.note: Run means go — do all my steps, starting now.

advanced.label: Arrow
advanced.note: An arrow is one step, and it points the way the bee will go.

advanced.label: Order
advanced.note: The order is which step comes first. Change the order and you get a different program.

sort.title: Clear or Too Fuzzy?
sort.yesSay: Yes. A robot could do that one.
sort.noSay: Right. That one is too fuzzy for a robot.
sort.retry: Think about a robot trying to do it. Would it know exactly what to do?

items.note: Three is a number. A robot can count.
How much is a little bit? A robot has no idea.
One block, one colour. Nothing left to guess.
Clean up which things, and put them where?
Left is left. That one is exact.
Over where? A robot can't follow your finger.
Even people argue about that one.

items.text: Put the blue cup on the table.
items.note: What to pick up, and where to put it. That's a whole step.
It says how, not what. A robot needs a what.
Start, finish, and one step at a time.
Nicer to who? A robot can't decide that for you.

items.text: Wait until the light turns green.
items.note: Tricky, but yes — a robot can watch and wait for a thing to happen.

items.text: Bring me a snack I'd like.
items.note: It would have to know YOU. A step can't be about a favourite.
Two is a number. Jump, jump, done.

items.text: Put both shoes by the door.
items.note: Both shoes, one spot. Nothing to guess.
It sounds like an instruction, but it doesn't say what to do.
Big compared to what? Big is only a word until you say bigger than the cup.

steps.text: Put the bread in the toaster
Wait for it to pop up
A line going up, back to the start
Jelly on top of the peanut butter
A grown-up cuts it in half
Find the flower on the board
Tap the rest of the arrows in order
Watch the bee land on the flower
